summary: Adds IPv6 extensions to Mobile IPv4 so a dual-stack node can use both IPv4 and IPv6 home addresses and move between IPv4-only and dual-stack networks. This is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A traveling device can keep both an old-style and a new-style home address and still be reached as it moves around.

questions: how does mobile ipv4 support ipv6
what is an ipv6 prefix request extension
subtitle: Mobile IPv4 extensions that let a dual-stack device register IPv6 prefixes over IPv4 signaling and keep both address families as it moves.

tldr.problem: Mobile IPv4 keeps an IPv4 node reachable as it moves, but a node that also has IPv6 addresses has no way to keep those reachable through the same mechanism.
tldr.mechanism: Three new skippable Mobile IPv4 extensions let a mobile node register IPv6 home prefixes with its home agent and choose whether IPv6 traffic is tunneled to its IPv4 home address or its care-of address. The signaling stays IPv4.
tldr.outcome: Dual-stack nodes can roam across IPv4-only and dual-stack networks with one mobility protocol and without upgrading every network node to IPv6. Mobile IPv6 style route optimization is not possible.

today: RFC 5454 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Goals and Scope
sections.content:
Mobile IPv4 (RFC 3344) lets a mobile node with an IPv4 address keep communicating while it moves. This RFC extends it so a node with both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses can keep communicating through any of its addresses while moving in IPv4 or dual-stack networks.

The central idea is to separate the Mobile IPv4 signaling from the IP version of the traffic it tunnels. The signaling still runs over IPv4, yet it can set up both IPv4 and IPv6 tunnels over IPv4.

Two aims are named. It becomes a transition mechanism, allowing automated but controlled tunneling of IPv6 over IPv4, so networks can migrate without upgrading all nodes at once. More importantly, dual-stack nodes can use one protocol to handle the movement of both stacks.

The goals are registration of IPv6 home prefixes in addition to the IPv4 home address, with static and dynamic prefix delegation. A non-goal is registration of IPv6 care-of addresses. Mobile IPv6 (RFC 3775) route optimization is not possible, because Mobile IPv4 signaling does not provide it.
sections.plainLanguage: One travel pass, the old kind, now also covers the new kind of address. Your mail finds you wherever you go, but it still goes via home first.

sections.title: Implicit and Explicit Modes
sections.content:
Following the Network Mobility specification (RFC 3963), there are two modes. In implicit mode the mobile node sends no IPv6 prefix request extensions. The home agent finds the node's IPv6 prefixes by some mechanism not defined here. All IPv6 traffic MUST then be encapsulated over the IPv4 tunnel between the node's IPv4 home address and the home agent's address, so it is transparent to any foreign agent.

In explicit mode IPv6 bindings are signaled. The mobile node includes one or more IPv6 prefix request extensions in its registration request, and the home agent returns IPv6 prefix reply extensions to accept or reject each one. In co-located mode, the node can also say whether IPv6 traffic should be tunneled to its care-of address or its home address. The rest of the RFC mainly defines explicit mode.
sections.plainLanguage: Either the home office already knows which new-style addresses are yours, or you tell it on a form and it stamps each line accepted or rejected.

sections.title: The Three Extensions
sections.content:
All three are skippable extensions in the short format of RFC 3344, using type 152 (the DSMIPv4 extension) and distinguished by a subtype.

  • IPv6 Prefix Request (subtype 1, length 18) goes in a registration request. It carries a Prefix Length and a sixteen-byte Mobile IPv6 Network Prefix. Bits beyond the prefix length MUST be zero.
  • IPv6 Prefix Reply (subtype 2, length 20) goes in a registration reply. It adds a Code and a Reserved byte. A prefix length of 255 means the prefix field holds a link-local address.
  • IPv6 Tunneling Mode (subtype 3, length 2) goes in a request to say IPv6 traffic can be tunneled to the care-of address.

The reply Code values are 0 (accepted, IPv6 tunneled to the home address), 1 (accepted, tunneled to the care-of address), 8 (rejected, reason unspecified) and 9 (rejected, administratively prohibited).
sections.plainLanguage: There are three little forms: one asks to register a new-style address block, one answers yes or no, and one says where to deliver the mail.

sections.title: Registration Handling
sections.content:
A mobile node MAY include one or more prefix request extensions, and MAY include exactly one tunneling mode extension when it uses co-located care-of address mode. These must sit after the registration request header and before the mobile-home authentication extension, so authentication covers them.

Because the extensions are skippable, a reply with no prefix reply extension, to a request that had a prefix request, means the home agent does not support them. The mobile node then SHOULD continue as plain Mobile IPv4. The reply header code takes priority: if it is a reject code, all prefix requests are rejected. If it is an accept code, a prefix reply with a reject code rejects only that prefix.

For each valid prefix request, the home agent SHOULD return a matching reply, never more than one per prefix. It must check that registered prefixes do not overlap and must not show them as on-link to any other node. Foreign agent operation is not affected.

The registration lifetime applies to all bindings, including IPv6 prefixes. A zero-lifetime request removes all bindings. A re-registration that leaves out some prefix request extensions deregisters those prefixes. Private care-of addresses can use Mobile IP NAT traversal (RFC 3519).
sections.plainLanguage: If the home office ignores the new form, you carry on the old way. If it says no to one address, your other addresses are not affected.

sections.title: Tunneling IPv6 Traffic
sections.content:
The home agent tracks each node's registered IPv6 prefixes and its tunneling mode. With no tunneling mode extension, it MUST tunnel IPv6 packets to the node's IPv4 home address, wrapped in a further IPv4 tunnel to the foreign agent. This keeps IPv6 routing invisible to a foreign agent without IPv6 support. With the extension, it SHOULD tunnel to the care-of address, though it MAY ignore the extension and use the home address.

When tunneling to the care-of address, the encapsulation negotiated for Mobile IPv4 is used: IP-in-IP follows RFC 4213, and GRE can also carry IPv6. Minimal Encapsulation (RFC 2004) cannot be used because it does not support an inner IPv6 header. A node using foreign agent care-of mode MUST NOT send the tunneling mode extension.

The IPv4 tunnel is treated as a single-hop link with link-local addresses as in RFC 4213. Implementations MUST support the Static Tunnel MTU approach, and the dynamic one is optional. Copying ECN and DSCP between headers is RECOMMENDED. IPv6 multicast membership messages (MLD) go through the home address tunnel, bypassing the foreign agent.
sections.plainLanguage: New-style mail travels inside an old-style envelope. Depending on the choice, the envelope is addressed to your home address or to where you are right now.

sections.title: Getting IPv6 Prefixes
sections.content:
How a prefix is allocated, and how a home agent decides to accept one, is out of scope. Local configuration or an authorization system such as Diameter may decide.

A node may use DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation (RFC 3633). If it is not attached directly to its home agent, it first registers its IPv4 home address, then forms a link-local IPv6 address. It sends a registration request with a prefix request whose prefix length is 255 and whose prefix field holds that link-local address. After a success reply it can send DHCPv6 messages, all tunneled between its IPv4 home address and the home agent. Once prefixes are delegated, it SHOULD register them in explicit mode.
sections.plainLanguage: To get a block of new-style addresses, you first check in with your old address, then ask the home office to hand you a block.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The specification works within the security rules of RFC 3344 and gives IPv6 prefixes the same level of security as IPv4 home addresses. Home agents MUST check reverse-tunneled IPv6 packets as RFC 3024 does for IPv4, where the outer source must be a registered care-of address. They MUST also check that the inner source is a registered IPv4 home address or IPv6 prefix, and otherwise SHOULD silently discard the packet and log a security exception.

IANA registered type 152 from the skippable range 128-255, created a DSMIPv4 subtype space (1, 2 and 3 defined, others by Expert Review), and a code space for prefix replies (0, 1, 8 and 9 defined; 2-7 reserved for accept, 10-255 for reject).
sections.plainLanguage: The home office checks that the return address on every parcel really belongs to you, and throws out forgeries.

fields.name: Prefix Length
fields.desc: 255 means the field holds a link-local address.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zero from sender, ignored by receiver.

fields.name: Mobile IPv6 Network Prefix
fields.desc: Sixteen-byte prefix; low-order bits beyond the length are zero.

items.label: Accepted, tunnel to HoA
items.desc: IPv6 is tunneled to the IPv4 home address.

items.label: Accepted, tunnel to CoA
items.desc: IPv6 is tunneled to the care-of address.
